Souza, 1962. | | Painted in 1962, a period marking a pivotal shift in Souza's artistic development, this masterpiece, Untitled (Head), stands as a defining moment in his career, bridging the visual languages of his 1950s and 1960s periods. Created during his celebrated Gallery One years, the work embodies both an aesthetic breakthrough and a testament to Souza's rise as a leading figure in contemporary art. | | After leaving India for London in 1949, Souza endured several years of hardship before establishing himself as a vital voice within postwar British art. His perseverance culminated in widespread recognition by the late 1950s, notably with his first major solo exhibition at Gallery One in 1959. Organised by Victor Musgrave, this landmark show marked Souza's emergence on the international stage. Musgrave's vision proved instrumental in shaping the global recognition of modern Indian art. He was among the first to exhibit artists such as Sayed Haider Raza, Akbar Padamsee, Tyeb Mehta, Paritosh Sen, Avinash Chandra, Anwar Jalal Shemza, Ram Kumar, Laxman Pai, Maqbool Fida Husain, and Souza himself, an audacious and pioneering gesture that redefined the visibility of South Asian modernists abroad. | | Throughout his career, Souza sustained an unyielding commitment to experimentation. His portraits of the 1950s are distinguished by assertive cross-hatched lines, while by the early 1960s his approach had evolved toward radical distortion, transforming faces into complex, mutated forms. The present lot stands as a compelling testament to this evolution, an image where intensity, audacity, and emotion converge. | | "I have created a new kind of face... I have drawn the physiognomy way beyond Picasso, in completely new terms. And I am still a figurative painter... [Picasso] stumped them and the whole of the western world into shambles. When you examine the face, the morphology, I am the only artist who has taken it a step further." (F. N. Souza quoted in Y. Dalmia, 'A Passion for the Human Figure', The Making of Modern Indian Art: The Progressives, Oxford University Press, New Delhi, 2001, p. 94). | | As theatre director Ebrahim Alkazi, who lived with Souza in London during the 1950s, observed "Souza has despised artists who have merely played with the fire of art, warmed their hands over its embers. Alkazi, Souza's Seasons in Hell Art Heritage, Vol. 6, New Delhi, 1986–87, p. 76). | | Untitled (Head) captures Souza's artistic inferno. The painting channels his inner turmoil and relentless drive into a primal, distorted portrait, where exaggerated, disjointed features and heavy cross-hatching reject traditional aesthetics. Aggressive black lines and a stark palette transform the face into a grotesque icon, a visceral commentary on suffering and the raw physicality of existence. | | Here, Souza's exploration of the human condition reaches an uncompromising intensity. It conveys anguish and post-war existential anxiety while offering a critique of societal hypocrisy. The painting presents a profound inquiry into identity and offers a daring critique of the role and meaning of art.

Siltan Ali., New Delhi: LKA, 1983, n.p. | | Often described as the voice of the 'Tribal Spirit' in modern Indian art, Ali forged a singular path within Indian modernism, embracing figuration at a moment when abstraction had come to characterise the path of Modern Indian art. Ali's pictorial world depicts a fascination with the vitality of nature and humanity, what he once described as 'a great fecund reality in its many varied and complex manifestations.' (J Sultan Ali in J. Sultan Ali: A Figurative Painter with a Conviction, S A Krishnan published in Lalit Kala Contemporary, Vol xxxiv No 1). Seeking a style that was uniquely his own, Ali found inspiration in the vibrancy of Indian tribal art, a visual language distinct from classical tradition, and began engaging deeply with the communities that sustained it. | | His compositions are tightly knit yet often agitated, revealing a dynamic fusion of designs, colours, lines, and forms. The long, slender contours and angular geometry of his figures mark his departure from Western academic perspective, instead drawing on the carpet perspective of Indian and Persian miniature traditions, where his figures unfold in lyrical harmony. | | Among the recurring motifs in his oeuvre, the Nandi (bull), seen here in the left section of the composition, receding into the middle ground, stands as the most significant. The artist's connection to this symbol traces back to his transformative encounter with a monumental stone bull in Devanahalli, near Kolar in Karnataka, 'I saw a stone bull, it was like an elephant, an animal which was at once beautiful, powerful and fierce.' (J Sultan Ali in A Personal vision of Tribal and Folklore, S A Krishnan, Published in Lalit Kala Contemporary, April 1980). For Ali, the bull became an embodiment of virility, energy, and sacred continuity, inextricably tied to India's mythic and tribal imagination. While rooted in folklore, Ali's work was never imitative, instead, it reinterpreted those sources into a modern idiom uniquely his own. As he noted, "I did take off from this vital source, (...) my Nandi is essentially my own." (ibid.) | | Ali's engagement with Indian aesthetics within his oeuvre extended to the rasas, or emotional essences, that underpin traditional art theory. The rasas is a concept in Indian arts characterising the aesthetic flavour of any visual art. Ali was particularly drawn to the Bhayānaka (fear) and Vīra (courage) rasas, sentiments that fill his works with a powerful and primal spiritual energy. In the present lot, the artist employs rich, resonant hues of yellow, brown, and red to depict distorted puppet-like faces, elongated mouths, and exaggerated bodily forms that pay homage to folk art traditions. Human and animal creatures fill and crowd the canvas, their forms merging in a dynamic, almost monstrous interplay, shaping a composition that is at once grotesque and picturesque. | | This work captures the cycle from life to death and the tension between myth and life, which exist in constant dialogue, shaping the rhythms of human experience. For Ali, art was a 'design-oriented interpretation of nature' (ibid.), a means of expressing the timeless cycles of existence that connect the human and the cosmic. Untitled (Life Cycle Cradle to Grave) stands as a powerful testament to his vision, where tribal memory, folklore, and modern sensibility converge into a singular visual language filled with the mythic and the everyday. The work invites reflection on the universality and cyclicality of life, illustrating how existence unfolds physically and spiritually. | | Born in Mumbai, Ali trained at the Government College of Fine Art in Chennai. Over his prolific career, he exhibited widely, with notable showings at the Lalit Kala Akademi, the Venice Biennale, the São Paulo Biennial, and the India Triennale in New Delhi. | | For another work by the artist sold on these premises see, Modern & Contemporary South Asian Art, 10th December 2024, lot 5.

provenance: Property from a private collection, London. | Acquired from the artist. | | 'When we look at these creatures (horses), we must remember that the animal is not the subject of Husain's paintings: it is the daemonic principle that he depicts, and to him it is neither good nor bad.' Richard Bartholomew in Maqbool Fida Husain, by K. Bikram Singh, pg. 177. | | Husain's Untitled (Ashvamedha & Six Horses) is a commanding meditation on power, sacrifice, and transcendence. Painted almost entirely in modulations of white, with only the faintest breath of blue animating the surface, this monumental work demonstrates Husain's ability to create visual drama through restraint. The large horizontal composition stages a compelling tableau; on the left sits a regal figure, perhaps a swami or king, enthroned upon a raised takht, presiding over the ceremonial Ashvamedha, while six horses surge dynamically across the plane, embodying energy, vitality, and divine force. | | The Ashvamedha, an ancient Vedic ritual of royal consecration, was traditionally performed to assert a monarch's sovereignty and cosmic legitimacy. A sacred horse, representing the spirit of the king, was set free to wander for a year, followed by warriors who protected it. Upon its return, the horse was ritually sacrificed, symbolising renewal, dominion, and the cyclical power of life and death. Husain, ever attuned to the mythic and the allegorical, revisits this potent symbol not as literal narration but as an abstracted visual metaphor for creation, conquest, and spiritual release. | | The presence of six horses rather than one intensifies the drama of the composition. In Vedic and later Indian thought, the horse signifies strength, speed, and divine vitality, attributes associated with Surya, the sun god, whose chariot is drawn by seven horses, each representing a ray of light. Husain's choice of six may allude to the balance between motion and control, matter and spirit, the threshold between the earthly and the celestial. The horses, rendered in sweeping, angular contours, seem to explode from the stillness of the seated figure, their fluid forms evoking both animal musculature and the rhythmic dynamism of Husain's brush. | | Executed entirely in tones of white, with hints of pale blue defining shadow and depth, the work exudes a meditative luminosity. The limited palette strips away ornamentation, allowing the viewer to confront the essence of form and movement. White, for Husain, often carried associations of purity, transcendence, and the spiritual void, a state of potential rather than completion. The faint blue undertone introduces a subtle coolness, invoking air, space, and divinity, and tempering the heat of mythic intensity with calm reflection. | | Stylistically, the painting bears all the hallmarks of Husain's mature idiom: the bold simplification of line, the monumental treatment of subject, and the fusion of modernist abstraction with classical Indian themes. The king or swami, rendered in his quintessential pose atop the takht, acts as both participant and observer, an axis of stillness around which the elemental forces of the horses revolve. Through this juxtaposition, Husain transforms an ancient ritual into a timeless allegory of human ambition, creative energy and spiritual aspiration. | | In Untitled (Ashvamedha & Six Horses), Husain achieves a synthesis of myth and modernity, of motion and stillness. The work exemplifies his lifelong engagement with India's civilizational narratives and his gift for recasting them in a language both contemporary and universal. Here, the Ashvamedha is not merely an emblem of royal might, but a profound reflection on the eternal cycles of power, sacrifice, and renewal.
subject_matter: horses, king, takht, Ashvamedha, energy, vitality, power, sacrifice, motion, spirituality, abstraction

Educated initially in conventional academic painting, Abanindranath soon became dissatisfied with Western academic methods, seeking instead an art that would express Indian cultural identity, spiritual values, and indigenous aesthetic traditions. He drew inspiration from Mughal miniatures, Rajput painting, and folk art, synthesizing these into a style that was both nationalist in vision and deeply lyrical. | | Abanindranath was also profoundly influenced by East Asian techniques, particularly Japanese brushwork and the morotai method, which emphasizes soft tonal washes and subtle gradations of colour.
